questions.prompt: Lesson 1 says one single property is the biggest adjustment for anyone coming from bash or cmd.exe. What is that property, and why does it matter?
options: PowerShell's pipeline passes real .NET objects between commands, not plain text, so a later stage can read a real property instead of parsing printed output
PowerShell's pipeline formats every command's output as an aligned table automatically, which is what makes a script reliable
PowerShell's pipeline requires every cmdlet to be named Verb-Noun before it can be piped to another cmdlet
PowerShell's pipeline runs every stage at the same time in parallel rather than left to right
PowerShell's pipeline only works between two cmdlets that come from the same module
PowerShell's pipeline automatically retries a failed stage up to three times before giving up
questions.explain: Lesson 1's core claim, made concrete across Chapter 2, is that PowerShell's pipe operator hands the next command the real object a cmdlet produced, with every property intact, not the text you'd see printed to a console. That's exactly why Sort-Object CPU or Where-Object {$_.CPU -gt 100} work reliably later in the course: CPU is a genuine property on the object, never text that has to be parsed back out.
questions.distractorExplain: Auto-formatting for display is real, but it's a separate, later idea (Lesson 7's Format-Table) and it doesn't change what actually flows through the pipe — objects move through unformatted the whole way; formatting only happens at the point something is rendered for a human to read on screen.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: piping anything into ________() lists its real TypeName plus every property and method it actually has, instead of you having to guess from what the console happened to display.
questions.explain: Get-Member is Lesson 5's answer to 'what type is this, really?' — $serverName | Get-Member prints the object's true TypeName (e.g. System.String) and every property and method actually available on it, which is also exactly how Lesson 7 later proves that Get-Process output is a real object, not formatted text that merely looks like a table.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about PowerShell cmdlet naming and parameters, per Chapter 1.
options: Every cmdlet follows a Verb-Noun pattern, e.g. Get-ChildItem or Stop-Service
A switch parameter like -Recurse requires a value, e.g. you must write -Recurse $true for it to do anything
Named parameters are the safer choice for a saved script, because they don't silently break if arguments get reordered
PowerShell only recognizes two approved verbs across every cmdlet: Get and Set
A positional parameter's value is supplied by order, relying on the cmdlet's expected argument sequence instead of a parameter name
questions.explain: Every cmdlet is Verb-Noun by deliberate design (Lesson 3), and named parameters are self-documenting and order-independent, which is why the course writes scripts with them almost everywhere from Chapter 3 on. A switch parameter like -Recurse needs no value at all — just its presence turns the behavior on. PowerShell maintains dozens of approved verbs (Get, Set, New, Remove, Start, Stop, Restart, and more), not just two. Positional parameters do rely on supplying values in the order the cmdlet expects, which is exactly why they're riskier in a saved script.

questions.prompt: Match each Chapter 1 tool to what it actually is.
left: VS Code with the PowerShell extension
right: Searches installed cmdlets by verb and/or noun when you don't know the exact name
Legacy split-pane script editor, Windows PowerShell 5.1 only, no longer actively developed
A read-eval-print loop good for a quick one-liner, with no real editing and nothing saved when it closes
The current real standard for writing reusable scripts, with syntax highlighting, IntelliSense, and a debugger
questions.explain: The console is a disposable read-eval-print loop, good only for a quick command. The ISE is Microsoft's legacy script editor, still found on older servers but no longer developed and limited to Windows PowerShell 5.1. VS Code with the PowerShell extension is the actively developed real standard for anything you'll save or rerun. Get-Command searches installed cmdlets by verb and/or noun, which is how Lesson 4 finds a cmdlet you don't already know the name of.

questions.prompt: What do $a and $b actually contain after this runs, and why?
options: $a is the string "53" and $b is the integer 8, because quoting "5" made it a string, and + concatenates whenever either side is text
$a and $b are both the integer 8, because PowerShell always converts a quoted number back into a real number before doing math
$a and $b are both the string "53", because + always concatenates regardless of whether either side is quoted
This throws an error, because PowerShell doesn't allow mixing a quoted and an unquoted number in the same script
questions.explain: PowerShell is dynamically typed: "5" becomes a [string] because of the quotes, so + concatenates it with 3 to produce "53". 5 + 3, with no quotes on either side, stays numeric and produces the integer 8. Lesson 5 flags this exact pair as the first thing to check when a script's output looks wrong — a value may have silently picked up the wrong type.

questions.prompt: Inside the Where-Object stage, what does $_ actually refer to, and why does .CPU work reliably on it?
options: $_ is each process object flowing through the pipeline in turn, and .CPU works because CPU is a real property on that object, not parsed text
$_ is the previous command's printed console text, and .CPU extracts a column out of it by counting character positions
$_ is a fixed global variable that always holds the very first process Get-Process returned
$_ only has meaning inside Sort-Object; inside Where-Object it is undefined
questions.explain: Inside a script block passed to Where-Object or ForEach-Object, $_ refers to the current object flowing through the pipeline at that point, one at a time. Because Get-Process hands forward real Process objects, .CPU reads an actual property on that object — it isn't text being sliced apart, which is exactly Lesson 6's point about $_ and the object pipeline.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Where-Object, Select-Object, and ForEach-Object, per Lesson 8.
options: Where-Object decides, per object, whether that object continues down the pipeline, without changing the object itself
Select-Object can narrow which properties survive, or limit how many objects pass through, regardless of what condition they meet
ForEach-Object decides which objects qualify to continue — the same job Where-Object does
ForEach-Object runs an action against every object that reaches it, often for a side effect rather than new pipeline output
Select-Object filters out objects that fail to meet a condition, the same way Where-Object does
questions.explain: Where-Object is strictly a yes/no filter per object. Select-Object either narrows which properties an object carries forward or limits row count (-First/-Last), without asking whether an object 'qualifies.' ForEach-Object runs code against every object that arrives, typically for a side effect like printing a line — it neither filters (that's Where-Object's job) nor reshapes properties (that's Select-Object's job).

questions.code: Get-Process | Format-Table Name, CPU -AutoSize | Select-Object CPU
questions.prompt: Why doesn't this reliably hand back the CPU property, per Lesson 7?
options: Format-Table converts the pipeline into display-only formatting instructions, not the original Process objects, so Select-Object afterward has nothing real left to select from
Select-Object can only ever be used immediately after Get-Process, never any later stage in a pipeline
CPU is spelled differently once Format-Table renders it, so Select-Object can't find a matching property name
Format-Table deletes every property on the object except whichever ones -AutoSize happens to widen
questions.explain: Format-Table is display-only: it converts whatever reaches it into formatting data meant for the console to render, not the original Process objects anymore. That's exactly why Microsoft's own guidance — and this lesson's rule — is that a Format-* cmdlet should be the last thing in a pipeline. Get-Process | Select-Object Name, CPU instead keeps real objects the whole way through and reliably exposes CPU.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Get-Process | Sort-Object CPU -________ sorts processes by CPU from highest to lowest, instead of the default ascending order.
questions.explain: Sort-Object's default order is ascending; the -Descending switch reverses it. Lesson 9 also notes that sorting by more than one property sorts by the first property first, using later properties only to break ties within each group.

questions.prompt: A pipeline needs to keep only stopped services, show just their names, and print each one. Put these stages in the correct left-to-right order, per Lesson 8's three-cmdlet pattern.
items: Get-Service retrieves every service on the machine
Where-Object {$_.Status -eq 'Stopped'} keeps only the stopped services
Select-Object Name keeps just the Name property
ForEach-Object { Write-Host $_.Name } prints each remaining name
questions.explain: Lesson 8's one decisive question applied in order: first decide which objects survive (Where-Object), then decide what those surviving objects look like (Select-Object), then do something to each one (ForEach-Object) — filter, then shape, then act, exactly as Lesson 8's worked example chains them.

questions.code:
.\check-disk-space.ps1
# File check-disk-space.ps1 cannot be loaded because running scripts
# is disabled on this system.
questions.prompt: What actually causes this error, and what is the real, common fix a DBA would use on a machine they control, per Lesson 10?
options: PowerShell's execution policy blocks scripts by default as a safety setting; Set-ExecutionPolicy RemoteSigned -Scope CurrentUser is the common practical fix
The script file itself is corrupted and needs to be re-saved with a .txt extension before it will run
PowerShell requires every script, including ones you wrote yourself, to carry a trusted digital signature under any policy
The leading .\ is invalid syntax here and must be removed before the script will run at all
questions.explain: Execution policy is a safety setting, not a bug — it blocks scripts from running by default so a malicious .ps1 can't execute just by being double-clicked. RemoteSigned, applied with -Scope CurrentUser, is the practical middle ground almost every DBA actually runs: local scripts run freely, while anything downloaded from the internet needs a trusted signature first.

questions.prompt: Match each Lesson 11 term to what it actually does.
right: Matches one variable against a list of discrete known values, with a fallback case when nothing matches
An additional condition checked only if the prior if was false
questions.explain: PowerShell uses letter-based comparison operators because < and > are already reserved for output redirection — -eq is equality, -gt is greater-than. switch states one variable once and lists discrete values underneath it, with default as its fallback, the equivalent of a final else. elseif adds another condition that's only checked once the prior if already failed.

questions.prompt: A script needs to retry a database connection up to 5 times, stopping as soon as it succeeds. Which loop fits best, per Lesson 12, and why?
options: while, because the number of attempts actually needed isn't known in advance — it keeps going only as long as its condition stays true
foreach, because you already have a fixed list of 5 attempts ready to iterate over
for, because retrying a connection is fundamentally about iterating over an existing collection of attempts
switch, because there are exactly 5 discrete attempt values to match against
questions.explain: while is the right tool when you're waiting for something to become true without knowing the iteration count in advance — exactly a retry loop. foreach needs a collection you already have, which a not-yet-successful connection attempt isn't; for is for counting a controlled number of passes, not waiting on a condition; switch matches one variable against known values, not retrying anything.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about PowerShell functions, per Lesson 13.
options: A function's parameter can be given an explicit type, like [int]$ThresholdGB, which rejects the wrong kind of value at call time
A parameter given a default value, like $ThresholdGB = 20, must still be supplied by every caller or the function errors
Functions are named Verb-Noun by the same convention built-in cmdlets use, for the same discoverability reason
Get-Verb lists the approved verbs you can check your own function's name against
A function can only be called after the entire script file it's defined in has finished running top to bottom
questions.explain: Typed parameters reject a mismatched value immediately rather than failing confusingly later. The whole point of a default value is that callers may omit it — Test-DiskSpace with no arguments at all still worked in Lesson 13's example. Verb-Noun naming for your own functions is the same discoverability pattern as built-in cmdlets, and Get-Verb checks whether a verb is on the approved list. A function becomes callable as soon as it's defined (by running or dot-sourcing the script), not only after the whole file finishes.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of safely running a brand-new .ps1 script, on a machine you control, in the correct order per Lesson 10.
items: Check the current policy with Get-ExecutionPolicy
Allow local scripts with Set-ExecutionPolicy RemoteSigned -Scope CurrentUser
Run the script using its relative path, e.g. .\check-disk-space.ps1
Read the console output or any error message it produces
questions.explain: Lesson 10 walks this exact sequence: confirm the current execution policy first, loosen it to RemoteSigned for your account if scripts are blocked, run the script with the required .\ prefix since the current directory isn't searched by default, and then read what it actually produced.

questions.prompt: What does dbatools primarily add to SQL Server administration, compared to using SSMS alone?
options: A free, open-source PowerShell module that scripts and automates the repetitive, multi-server DBA work SSMS's GUI was never designed to automate
A replacement graphical interface for SSMS with a modernized look
A built-in backup encryption algorithm that doesn't exist anywhere in SQL Server itself
A licensing tool that unlocks SQL Server Standard Edition features inside Express Edition
A cloud-only service that can only run T-SQL from inside Azure Cloud Shell
A direct replacement for SQL Server Agent that removes the need for scheduled jobs
questions.explain: dbatools is a free, open-source, community-maintained PowerShell module purpose-built for SQL Server administration. It doesn't replace SSMS for interactive, one-server-at-a-time work — it replaces the repetitive work SSMS's GUI was never designed to automate, like checking the same setting across fifty servers or running the same maintenance step every night.
questions.distractorExplain: The closest wrong option is the 'replacement GUI for SSMS' framing — dbatools genuinely is SQL-Server-administration tooling, but it's a scripting module layered on top of PowerShell, not an interactive interface meant to replace SSMS. SSMS stays the tool for interactive, one-off work; dbatools automates the surrounding repetitive work instead.

questions.prompt: What does $results actually contain, and why does that matter for what you can do with it next?
options: Real PowerShell objects representing each row, so $results can immediately be piped through Where-Object or looped with foreach
Plain text formatted exactly as it would appear in SSMS's results grid
A single string containing the entire query's output concatenated together
Nothing at all, until a Format-Table cmdlet is called on it
questions.explain: Invoke-DbaQuery hands results back as real PowerShell objects, not text you'd have to parse. Because of that, everything from Chapters 1-3 applies immediately — piping through Where-Object to filter, looping with foreach to act on each row, or wrapping the whole thing in a function, exactly as Lesson 16 demonstrates.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Az cmdlets follow the naming pattern Verb-Az<Service><Noun> — ________ is the one cmdlet that opens an authenticated, browser-based Azure sign-in session.
questions.explain: Connect-AzAccount, from the Az.Accounts piece of the Az module, opens a browser window for interactive sign-in and then prints which account, subscription, and tenant you landed in — the one command Lesson 15 identifies as opening an authenticated Azure session.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about connecting to Azure from PowerShell, per Lesson 15.
options: Connect-AzAccount opens an interactive, browser-based sign-in
Azure Cloud Shell requires the Az module to already be installed locally before it can be used
Set-AzContext switches which subscription is active for the current session
Disconnect-AzAccount matters in particular on a shared machine, to avoid leaving a signed-in session with production access exposed
AzureRM is the actively developed, currently recommended module for writing new Azure scripts
questions.explain: Connect-AzAccount opens the interactive sign-in, and Set-AzContext switches the active subscription afterward. Disconnect-AzAccount genuinely matters on a shared machine, the same way logging out of anything else does. Azure Cloud Shell needs no local Az install at all — it's already authenticated in the browser. AzureRM was retired in favor of Az; seeing Import-Module AzureRM in a script is a sign it needs updating.

questions.prompt: Lesson 18 wraps Test-BackupAge's original single line in this try/catch. What problem does it actually fix?
options: Without it, one unreachable server throws an error that stops the entire script, never checking any server listed after it — the try/catch lets the outer foreach move on to the next server instead
It makes Invoke-DbaQuery run noticeably faster by skipping a connection attempt to any unreachable server
It changes the underlying T-SQL query itself to exclude unreachable servers from the result set
It is purely cosmetic — without it the script behaves identically but prints a less friendly error message
questions.explain: Reading the original script closely surfaces a real gap: Invoke-DbaQuery throws if a server is down, and with no error handling that error stops the entire script before it ever reaches the servers after it in the list. try runs the risky line; catch runs instead of crashing; return exits only this one call to the function, so the outer foreach over $servers keeps going untouched — a safe, additive fix found by reading carefully, not by skimming.
